newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ailing Yeltsin keen to return to political fray.
newsitem.headline: Ailing Yeltsin keen to return to political fray.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin is very keen to return to Russia's political fray but has still not recovered fully from double pneumonia, his press secretary said on Friday.

The Kremlin has not released any photos or videos of the president in more than two weeks, and the first public event Yeltsin was scheduled to attend, a summit of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), has been postponed.
In parliament, the president faced a new test as deputies continued debating into the evening whether to approve his government's 1997 budget.

His bitter foes the communists, who launched an initiative this week to oust him, said their support for the budget would depend on the government's readiness to pay huge wage and pension arrears swiftly to millions of Russians.
Yeltsin kept a low profile as proceedings began in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
His spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the 65-year-old president met Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais at the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow where he is recovering.

"The president clearly has a huge, burning desire to return as soon as possible to carrying out his duties in full...and it is clear he has retained his characteristic political will," he told a news briefing.

"But on the other hand the president has not fully recovered after his very serious illness, double pneumonia. His physical condition is not good enough to expect him to force his return to the Kremlin," Yastrzhembsky said.
A brief visit to the Kremlin on Wednesday, less than two full days after he left hospital, failed to dispel doubts over Yeltsin's health and his ability to rule.
CIS officials did not cite Yeltsin's health as a reason on Friday for postponing a January 29 Moscow summit of leaders from the former Soviet republics but they said Yeltsin had agreed to the delay.
Yeltsin's continued absence from the political scene prompted the Duma to debate a motion on Wednesday on trying to oust him, and discussions are set to continue next month.
The president, who was re-elected last July, was out of the Kremlin for most of the second half of 1996 with heart problems, and he had a bypass operation on November 5.
The communists, the largest force in the Duma, had another chance to attack Yeltsin and the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the budget debate.
Deputies have approved three readings of the budget. The government, facing huge economic problems, has agreed to raise spending in several areas in efforts to win over the opposition.
Yeltsin also faces major foreign policy challenges this year, including a dispute with NATO over its plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott met Chernomyrdin in Moscow to prepare for the prime minister's trip to the United States next month, Russian news agencies said.

NATO sources in Brussels said Talbott had also brought with him new proposals for a deal cutting the huge U.S. advantage in sea-based strategic nuclear missiles as part of efforts to win Russian support for NATO's plans to expand eastwards.
Also on Friday, security was stepped up in Chechnya before Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections in the region, but officials said trouble could not be ruled out.
